fp2_matrices2_eigen.description: Find every real eigenvalue and a matching non-zero eigenvector of a 2 by 2 or 3 by 3 matrix.

sections.title: How do I recognise an eigenvector?
sections.label: One invariant direction
sections.intro: Matrix multiplication can turn a vector. An eigenvector keeps the same line through the origin after multiplication, even when its orientation reverses.

blocks.html: Test \(A\boldsymbol v=\lambda\boldsymbol v\) with \(\boldsymbol v\ne\boldsymbol0\). If the image is zero, a non-zero original vector is still an eigenvector and the eigenvalue is \(0\).

figure.alt: The original vector and its image lie on the same line through the origin. The image points in the opposite direction, indicating a negative eigenvalue.
figure.caption: The original vector and its image lie on the same line through the origin. The image points in the opposite direction, indicating a negative eigenvalue.

blocks.html: The zero vector satisfies the equation for every scalar, so it cannot identify an eigenvalue. A vector with a zero component is allowed.
Find the scalar from a non-zero component and then check every row.

blocks.title: Read a negative multiplier
blocks.prompt: The vector \(\left(\begin{matrix}0\\1\end{matrix}\right)\) is an eigenvector of \(\left(\begin{matrix}3 & 0\\-14 & -4\end{matrix}\right)\). Find its eigenvalue.
blocks.hint: Compare every component. Do not divide by a zero component.
blocks.solution:
Computation gives \(\left(\begin{matrix}0\\-4\end{matrix}\right)\). Find the common factor relating that product to the original vector.

Using the second nonzero coordinate gives \(\lambda=-4\). The same scalar works in every row.

blocks.title: Check a third row
blocks.prompt: The vector \(\left(\begin{matrix}1\\0\\1\end{matrix}\right)\) is an eigenvector of \(\left(\begin{matrix}-3 & 0 & 8\\-4 & 1 & 4\\0 & 0 & 5\end{matrix}\right)\). Find its eigenvalue.
blocks.hint: Compare every component. Do not divide by a zero component.
blocks.solution:
Computation gives \(\left(\begin{matrix}5\\0\\5\end{matrix}\right)\). Find the common factor relating that product to the original vector.

Using the first nonzero coordinate gives \(\lambda=5\). The same scalar works in every row.

sections.title: Why does the determinant determine the eigenvalues?
sections.label: Find all eigenvalues
sections.intro: Moving \(\lambda\boldsymbol v\) to the left gives a homogeneous system. A non-zero solution can exist only when its coefficient matrix is singular.

blocks.html: Solve \(\det(\lambda I-A)=0\). This monic convention is convenient; \(\det(A-\lambda I)=0\) has exactly the same roots. Expand or factor before substituting any numeric eigenvalue.
Subtract the eigenvalue only on the main diagonal. Subtracting it from every entry changes the equations.
For a triangular matrix the roots are its diagonal entries.

blocks.title: Find two roots
blocks.prompt: Find every eigenvalue of \(\left(\begin{matrix}-11 & 12\\-6 & 7\end{matrix}\right)\).
blocks.hint: Subtract the unknown eigenvalue from the main diagonal before evaluating the determinant.
blocks.solution:
An eigenvalue makes \(A-\lambda I\) singular. The determinant equation is \(\lambda^{2} + 4 \lambda - 5=0\).

Factor this polynomial as \(\left(\lambda - 1\right) \left(\lambda + 5\right)=0\). Its real roots give the full set \(\left\{-5,1\right\}\).

sections.title: How do I find a non-zero eigenvector once I know the value?
sections.label: Solve an eigenspace
sections.intro: Insert one eigenvalue into \((A-\lambda I)\boldsymbol v=\boldsymbol0\). The independent rows determine ratios, and a free component sets the scale.

blocks.html: If \(\lambda\) is a distinct root of the characteristic polynomial, all eigenvectors for it are non-zero scalar multiples of one vector. One non-zero coordinate can be set to one provided you choose one that is actually free or nonzero.
If the row equations force one coordinate to be zero, it cannot be the coordinate you choose as one.
After back-substitution, verify the image of the actual vector claimed.

blocks.title: Normalise eigenvector scale
blocks.prompt: For \(A=\left(\begin{matrix}8 & -6\\12 & -10\end{matrix}\right)\), find an eigenvector for \(\lambda=2\) whose first component is 1.
blocks.hint: Use the known eigenvalue before solving for the unknown entries.
blocks.solution:
Set up the homogeneous system \(\left(\begin{matrix}6 & -6\\12 & -12\end{matrix}\right)\mathbf v=\mathbf0\). A free coordinate can be chosen because this coefficient matrix is singular.

Set the first component equal to one and back-substitute. This gives \(\left(\begin{matrix}1\\1\end{matrix}\right)\).

Multiplication gives \(\left(\begin{matrix}2\\2\end{matrix}\right)\), exactly \(2\) times the chosen vector.

blocks.title: Use the selected eigenvalue
blocks.prompt: For \(A=\left(\begin{matrix}6 & 0\\-16 & -2\end{matrix}\right)\), find an eigenvector for \(\lambda=6\) whose first component is 1.
blocks.hint: Use the known eigenvalue before solving for the unknown entries.
blocks.solution:
Set up the homogeneous system \(\left(\begin{matrix}0 & 0\\-16 & -8\end{matrix}\right)\mathbf v=\mathbf0\). A free coordinate can be chosen because this coefficient matrix is singular.

Set the first component equal to one and back-substitute. This gives \(\left(\begin{matrix}1\\-2\end{matrix}\right)\).

Multiplication gives \(\left(\begin{matrix}6\\-12\end{matrix}\right)\), exactly \(6\) times the chosen vector.

sections.title: What changes for a three-by-three matrix?
sections.label: Work in three dimensions
sections.intro: The definition does not change. The characteristic equation has degree three. A zero pattern can simplify finding a factor, for example a triangular block or a sparse row.

blocks.html: After finding all three real distinct eigenvalues, solve one homogeneous system per value. Two independent equations normally fix two components in terms of the third.
Matching a vector to a different eigenvalue changes the action even if the two columns are both correct individually.
Arrange your final output into matched pairs of a value and a non-zero vector.

blocks.title: Find three triangular roots
blocks.prompt: Find every eigenvalue of \(\left(\begin{matrix}1 & 2 & -1\\0 & 5 & 4\\0 & 0 & -6\end{matrix}\right)\).
blocks.hint: For a triangular matrix use the product of the diagonal terms.
blocks.solution:
The matrix \(A-\lambda I\) is triangular since only its diagonal has changed.

Its determinant is the product of the diagonal terms. It vanishes when \(1\), \(5\) or \(-6\) is subtracted.

sections.title: How can I check the complete spectrum quickly?
sections.label: Trace and determinant checks
sections.intro: The coefficients of the characteristic polynomial encode properties of the matrix. They are useful for spotting a missing eigenvalue or a sign error.

blocks.html: The sum of the three or two eigenvalues equals \(\operatorname{tr}(A)\) and their product equals \(\det A\). Check these after factoring.
Equal trace alone does not verify a set of eigenvalues. Use the determinant or substitute into the original characteristic equation as well.
If one eigenvalue is zero, its product with the others is zero. Do not divide by it to recover a missing value.

blocks.title: Audit a complete real spectrum
blocks.prompt: Find every eigenvalue of \(\left(\begin{matrix}-3 & 5 & -10\\0 & 2 & 8\\0 & 0 & 6\end{matrix}\right)\).
blocks.hint: Subtract the unknown eigenvalue from the main diagonal before evaluating the determinant.
blocks.solution:
An eigenvalue makes \(A-\lambda I\) singular. The determinant equation is \(\lambda^{3} - 5 \lambda^{2} - 12 \lambda + 36=0\).

Factor this polynomial as \(\left(\lambda - 6\right) \left(\lambda - 2\right) \left(\lambda + 3\right)=0\). Its real roots give the full set \(\left\{-3,2,6\right\}\).

examples.title: Read the common factor
examples.question: The vector \(\left(\begin{matrix}0\\1\end{matrix}\right)\) is an eigenvector of \(\left(\begin{matrix}-2 & 0\\14 & 5\end{matrix}\right)\). Find its eigenvalue.
solution: Computation gives \(\left(\begin{matrix}0\\5\end{matrix}\right)\). Find the common factor relating that product to the original vector.
Using the second nonzero coordinate gives \(\lambda=5\). The same scalar works in every row.

examples.title: The image can be zero
examples.question: The vector \(\left(\begin{matrix}2\\1\end{matrix}\right)\) is an eigenvector of \(\left(\begin{matrix}-3 & 6\\-3 & 6\end{matrix}\right)\). Find its eigenvalue.
solution: Computation gives \(\left(\begin{matrix}0\\0\end{matrix}\right)\). Find the common factor relating that product to the original vector.
Using the first nonzero coordinate gives \(\lambda=0\). The same scalar works in every row.

examples.title: A full two-dimensional characteristic equation
examples.question: Find every eigenvalue of \(\left(\begin{matrix}5 & -4\\8 & -7\end{matrix}\right)\).
solution: An eigenvalue makes \(A-\lambda I\) singular. The determinant equation is \(\lambda^{2} + 2 \lambda - 3=0\).
Factor this polynomial as \(\left(\lambda - 1\right) \left(\lambda + 3\right)=0\). Its real roots give the full set \(\left\{-3,1\right\}\).

examples.title: Normalise an allowed component
examples.question: For \(A=\left(\begin{matrix}-6 & 5\\-10 & 9\end{matrix}\right)\), find an eigenvector for \(\lambda=-1\) whose first component is 1.
solution: Set up the homogeneous system \(\left(\begin{matrix}-5 & 5\\-10 & 10\end{matrix}\right)\mathbf v=\mathbf0\). A free coordinate can be chosen because this coefficient matrix is singular.
Set the first component equal to one and back-substitute. This gives \(\left(\begin{matrix}1\\1\end{matrix}\right)\).
Multiplication gives \(\left(\begin{matrix}-1\\-1\end{matrix}\right)\), exactly \(-1\) times the chosen vector.

examples.title: A zero coordinate is allowed
examples.question: For \(A=\left(\begin{matrix}2 & 10\\0 & 7\end{matrix}\right)\), find an eigenvector for \(\lambda=2\) whose first component is 1.
solution: Set up the homogeneous system \(\left(\begin{matrix}0 & 10\\0 & 5\end{matrix}\right)\mathbf v=\mathbf0\). A free coordinate can be chosen because this coefficient matrix is singular.
Set the first component equal to one and back-substitute. This gives \(\left(\begin{matrix}1\\0\end{matrix}\right)\).
Multiplication gives \(\left(\begin{matrix}2\\0\end{matrix}\right)\), exactly \(2\) times the chosen vector.

examples.title: Use a triangular cubic
examples.question: Find every eigenvalue of \(\left(\begin{matrix}3 & 2 & -1\\0 & -2 & 4\\0 & 0 & 5\end{matrix}\right)\).
solution: The matrix \(A-\lambda I\) is triangular since only its diagonal has changed.
Its determinant is the product of the diagonal terms. It vanishes when \(3\), \(-2\) or \(5\) is subtracted.

examples.title: Check a three-value spectrum
examples.question: Find every eigenvalue of \(\left(\begin{matrix}-1 & 0 & 5\\-2 & 1 & 2\\0 & 0 & 4\end{matrix}\right)\).
solution: An eigenvalue makes \(A-\lambda I\) singular. The determinant equation is \(\lambda^{3} - 4 \lambda^{2} - \lambda + 4=0\).
Factor this polynomial as \(\left(\lambda - 4\right) \left(\lambda - 1\right) \left(\lambda + 1\right)=0\). Its real roots give the full set \(\left\{-1,1,4\right\}\).

extraPractice.title: Recover a three-component eigenvector
extraPractice.prompt: For \(A=\left(\begin{matrix}-4 & 5 & 1\\0 & 1 & 1\\0 & 0 & 2\end{matrix}\right)\), find an eigenvector for \(\lambda=-4\) whose first component is 1.
extraPractice.hint: Use the known eigenvalue before solving for the unknown entries.
extraPractice.solution:
Set up the homogeneous system \(\left(\begin{matrix}0 & 5 & 1\\0 & 5 & 1\\0 & 0 & 6\end{matrix}\right)\mathbf v=\mathbf0\). A free coordinate can be chosen because this coefficient matrix is singular.

Set the first component equal to one and back-substitute. This gives \(\left(\begin{matrix}1\\0\\0\end{matrix}\right)\).

Multiplication gives \(\left(\begin{matrix}-4\\0\\0\end{matrix}\right)\), exactly \(-4\) times the chosen vector.

extraPractice.title: Recognise a zero eigenvalue
extraPractice.prompt: Find every eigenvalue of \(\left(\begin{matrix}-1 & 2 & -1\\0 & 0 & 4\\0 & 0 & 6\end{matrix}\right)\).
extraPractice.hint: For a triangular matrix use the product of the diagonal terms.
extraPractice.solution:
The matrix \(A-\lambda I\) is triangular since only its diagonal has changed.

Its determinant is the product of the diagonal terms. It vanishes when \(-1\), \(0\) or \(6\) is subtracted.

extraPractice.title: Compare the image of a full vector
extraPractice.prompt: The vector \(\left(\begin{matrix}1\\0\\0\end{matrix}\right)\) is an eigenvector of \(\left(\begin{matrix}2 & 1 & 6\\0 & 3 & 6\\0 & 0 & 9\end{matrix}\right)\). Find its eigenvalue.
extraPractice.hint: Compare every component. Do not divide by a zero component.
extraPractice.solution:
Computation gives \(\left(\begin{matrix}2\\0\\0\end{matrix}\right)\). Find the common factor relating that product to the original vector.

Using the first nonzero coordinate gives \(\lambda=2\). The same scalar works in every row.

extraPractice.title: Solve a non-triangular characteristic equation
extraPractice.prompt: Find every eigenvalue of \(\left(\begin{matrix}-9 & 5\\-10 & 6\end{matrix}\right)\).
extraPractice.hint: Subtract the unknown eigenvalue from the main diagonal before evaluating the determinant.
extraPractice.solution:
An eigenvalue makes \(A-\lambda I\) singular. The determinant equation is \(\lambda^{2} + 3 \lambda - 4=0\).

Factor this polynomial as \(\left(\lambda - 1\right) \left(\lambda + 4\right)=0\). Its real roots give the full set \(\left\{-4,1\right\}\).

extraPractice.title: All three eigenvalues in any order
extraPractice.prompt: Find every eigenvalue of \(\left(\begin{matrix}14 & -16 & 11\\11 & -13 & 11\\6 & -6 & 9\end{matrix}\right)\).
extraPractice.hint: Subtract the unknown eigenvalue from the main diagonal before evaluating the determinant.
extraPractice.solution:
An eigenvalue makes \(A-\lambda I\) singular. The determinant equation is \(\lambda^{3} - 10 \lambda^{2} + 3 \lambda + 54=0\).

Factor this polynomial as \(\left(\lambda - 9\right) \left(\lambda - 3\right) \left(\lambda + 2\right)=0\). Its real roots give the full set \(\left\{-2,3,9\right\}\).

glossary.definition: A non-zero vector \(\boldsymbol v\) with \(A\boldsymbol v=\lambda\boldsymbol v\).
The scalar multiplier associated with an eigenvector.
\(\det(\lambda I-A)=0\).
The set of vectors solving the homogeneous system for one eigenvalue, including zero.
The sum of the diagonal entries.

revision.body: Use \(\det(\lambda I-A)=0\) for the values and \((A-\lambda I)\boldsymbol v=\boldsymbol0\) for their vectors. Verify by direct multiplication.
revision.checks:
• Did you find every distinct real eigenvalue?
  • What happens when an eigenvalue is zero?
  • Does each chosen scale produce a non-zero vector?
revision.examTip: Keep the vector paired with its eigenvalue and show where its free parameter comes from.

fp2_matrices2_algebra.description: Use eigenvectors to reason about the eigenvalues of matrix powers, inverses, shifts and polynomial expressions.

sections.title: Why does taking a power raise the eigenvalue to the same power?
sections.label: Repeated action
sections.intro: Starting on an eigenvector makes every application of the matrix a multiplication by the same scalar. The direction stays fixed even when that scalar is negative.

blocks.html: \(A^2\boldsymbol v=A(\lambda\boldsymbol v)=\lambda^2\boldsymbol v\) and in general \(A^n\boldsymbol v=\lambda^n\boldsymbol v\) for positive integer \(n\).
If \(\lambda<0\), an odd power keeps the negative sign. A sign change is part of the action on the vector.
Show at least one application of the definition before using the general rule.

blocks.title: Power of a signed eigenvalue
blocks.prompt: Suppose \(A\mathbf v=-3\mathbf v,\quad \mathbf v\ne\mathbf0\). Find the eigenvalue of \(A^{3}\) corresponding to \(\mathbf v\).
blocks.hint: Keep the same non-zero eigenvector while changing the matrix.
blocks.solution:
Apply \(A\) one step at a time. Every application multiplies this same direction by \(\lambda\).

\(A^n\mathbf v=A^{n-1}(\lambda\mathbf v)=\lambda^n\mathbf v\).

Substituting \(\lambda=-3\) gives the associated eigenvalue \(-27\).

blocks.title: Power on a 3D eigendirection
blocks.prompt: Suppose \(A\mathbf v=-2\mathbf v,\quad \mathbf v\ne\mathbf0\). Find the eigenvalue of \(A^{4}\) corresponding to \(\mathbf v\).
blocks.hint: Keep the same non-zero eigenvector while changing the matrix.
blocks.solution:
Apply \(A\) one step at a time. Every application multiplies this same direction by \(\lambda\).

\(A^n\mathbf v=A^{n-1}(\lambda\mathbf v)=\lambda^n\mathbf v\).

Substituting \(\lambda=-2\) gives the associated eigenvalue \(16\).

sections.title: When is the reciprocal eigenvalue rule allowed?
sections.label: Inverse action
sections.intro: An inverse matrix reverses the action of the original matrix. On the eigenvector line it must reverse multiplication by a nonzero number.

blocks.html: If \(A\) is invertible, then \(A^{-1}\boldsymbol v=\lambda^{-1}\boldsymbol v\). Justify \(\lambda\ne0\) from invertibility first.
A non-zero eigenvalue attached to the stated vector alone does not show the entire matrix is invertible. Other eigenvalues might be zero.
The same vector remains an eigenvector of every integer power whenever \(A\) is invertible.

blocks.title: Use the exact reciprocal
blocks.prompt: Suppose \(A\mathbf v=5\mathbf v,\quad \mathbf v\ne\mathbf0\) and \(A\) is invertible. Find the eigenvalue of \(A^{-1}\) corresponding to \(\mathbf v\).
blocks.hint: Keep the same non-zero eigenvector while changing the matrix.
blocks.solution:
Apply \(A^{-1}\) on the left of both sides of the original relation. The scalar still commutes with the matrix.

\(\mathbf v=\lambda A^{-1}\mathbf v\); as \(\lambda\ne0\), divide by \(\lambda\).

Substituting \(\lambda=5\) gives the associated eigenvalue \(\frac{1}{5}\).

sections.title: How does shifting a matrix change its eigenvalues?
sections.label: Identity shifts
sections.intro: The identity sends each vector to itself. Adding a multiple of the identity therefore adds its scalar multiplier to the action on every eigenvector.

blocks.html: \((aA+bI)\boldsymbol v=(a\lambda+b)\boldsymbol v\). In particular \(A-\mu I\) is singular when \(\mu\) equals an eigenvalue of \(A\).
Adding \(bI\) changes only the diagonal entries. Adding \(b\) to every entry is a different operation.
When matching the vector use the same orientation and components.

blocks.title: Shift a negative eigenvalue
blocks.prompt: Let \(A\boldsymbol v=-5\boldsymbol v\) for a non-zero vector. Find its eigenvalue for \(2A+6I\).
blocks.hint: Use that the identity leaves each vector unchanged.
blocks.solution:
Multiply the original scalar by \(2\). The identity term adds \(6\) times the original vector.

The combined multiplier is \(2\times(-5)+6=-4\).

blocks.title: Find a zero after shifting
blocks.prompt: Let \(A\boldsymbol v=3\boldsymbol v\) for a non-zero vector. Find its eigenvalue for \(3A-9I\).
blocks.hint: Use that the identity leaves each vector unchanged.
blocks.solution:
Multiply the original scalar by \(3\). The identity term adds \(-9\) times the original vector.

The combined multiplier is \(3\times(3)-9=0\).

sections.title: Can I evaluate a matrix expression by plugging in one eigenvalue?
sections.label: Polynomial action
sections.intro: If a problem asks what an expression in \(A\) does to one of its eigenvectors, each term acts by its own scalar on the same vector.

blocks.html: For a polynomial \(p\), \(p(A)\boldsymbol v=p(\lambda)\boldsymbol v\). For example, \((A^2-cA+dI)\boldsymbol v=(\lambda^2-c\lambda+d)\boldsymbol v\).
\(p(A)\) is still a matrix. Knowing its eigenvalue on one direction does not make the entire matrix equal to a scalar.
Check the scalar constant multiplies \(I\) when it is part of a matrix expression.

blocks.title: Evaluate the scalar polynomial
blocks.prompt: Suppose \(A\mathbf v=-3\mathbf v,\quad \mathbf v\ne\mathbf0\). Find the eigenvalue of \(A^2-A+2I\) corresponding to \(\mathbf v\).
blocks.hint: Keep the same non-zero eigenvector while changing the matrix.
blocks.solution:
Each matrix term acts on the same vector, so the scalar multipliers can be added.

Use \(A^2\mathbf v=\lambda^2\mathbf v\) and \(I\mathbf v=\mathbf v\).

Substituting \(\lambda=-3\) gives the associated eigenvalue \(14\).

sections.title: When can eigenvalue multipliers from two different matrices be combined?
sections.label: A shared vector
sections.intro: To multiply or add two matrices through their eigenvalues, the same vector must satisfy both eigenvector equations in the problem.

blocks.html: If \(A\boldsymbol v=\lambda\boldsymbol v\) and \(B\boldsymbol v=\mu\boldsymbol v\), then \((A+B)\boldsymbol v=(\lambda+\mu)\boldsymbol v\) and \(AB\boldsymbol v=\lambda\mu\boldsymbol v\). No general equality of \(AB\) and \(BA\) follows.
Choosing an eigenvalue from each matrix is not enough if their eigenvectors are different.
Apply the rightmost factor first and show that each step leaves the same direction.

blocks.title: Add and multiply the two actions
blocks.prompt: The same non-zero vector \(\boldsymbol v\) has eigenvalue \(-3\) for \(A\) and \(7\) for \(B\). Find its eigenvalue for \(AB\) and for \(A+B\).
blocks.hint: Check that both matrices act on the same vector.
blocks.solution:
The rightmost factor \(B\) multiplies the vector by \(7\). The next factor scales the result by \(-3\).

In the sum both multipliers are applied to the original vector. The combined values are \(-21\) and \(4\), respectively.

examples.title: Keep the sign of an odd power
examples.question: Suppose \(A\mathbf v=-2\mathbf v,\quad \mathbf v\ne\mathbf0\). Find the eigenvalue of \(A^{3}\) corresponding to \(\mathbf v\).
solution: Apply \(A\) one step at a time. Every application multiplies this same direction by \(\lambda\).
\(A^n\mathbf v=A^{n-1}(\lambda\mathbf v)=\lambda^n\mathbf v\).
Substituting \(\lambda=-2\) gives the associated eigenvalue \(-8\).

examples.title: Use a positive even power
examples.question: Suppose \(A\mathbf v=-3\mathbf v,\quad \mathbf v\ne\mathbf0\). Find the eigenvalue of \(A^{4}\) corresponding to \(\mathbf v\).
solution: Apply \(A\) one step at a time. Every application multiplies this same direction by \(\lambda\).
\(A^n\mathbf v=A^{n-1}(\lambda\mathbf v)=\lambda^n\mathbf v\).
Substituting \(\lambda=-3\) gives the associated eigenvalue \(81\).

examples.title: Reverse a negative action
examples.question: Suppose \(A\mathbf v=-3\mathbf v,\quad \mathbf v\ne\mathbf0\) and \(A\) is invertible. Find the eigenvalue of \(A^{-1}\) corresponding to \(\mathbf v\).
solution: Apply \(A^{-1}\) on the left of both sides of the original relation. The scalar still commutes with the matrix.
\(\mathbf v=\lambda A^{-1}\mathbf v\); as \(\lambda\ne0\), divide by \(\lambda\).
Substituting \(\lambda=-3\) gives the associated eigenvalue \(- \frac{1}{3}\).

examples.title: Shift the identity multiplier
examples.question: Let \(A\boldsymbol v=-3\boldsymbol v\) for a non-zero vector. Find its eigenvalue for \(2A+5I\).
solution: Multiply the original scalar by \(2\). The identity term adds \(5\) times the original vector.
The combined multiplier is \(2\times(-3)+5=-1\).

examples.title: A new eigenvalue can be zero
examples.question: Let \(A\boldsymbol v=4\boldsymbol v\) for a non-zero vector. Find its eigenvalue for \(2A-8I\).
solution: Multiply the original scalar by \(2\). The identity term adds \(-8\) times the original vector.
The combined multiplier is \(2\times(4)-8=0\).

examples.title: Combine three matrix terms
examples.question: Suppose \(A\mathbf v=-3\mathbf v,\quad \mathbf v\ne\mathbf0\). Find the eigenvalue of \(A^2+2I\) corresponding to \(\mathbf v\).
solution: Each matrix term acts on the same vector, so the scalar multipliers can be added.
Use \(A^2\mathbf v=\lambda^2\mathbf v\) and \(I\mathbf v=\mathbf v\).
Substituting \(\lambda=-3\) gives the associated eigenvalue \(11\).

examples.title: Apply two matrices to one direction
examples.question: The same non-zero vector \(\boldsymbol v\) has eigenvalue \(4\) for \(A\) and \(-5\) for \(B\). Find its eigenvalue for \(AB\) and for \(A+B\).
solution: The rightmost factor \(B\) multiplies the vector by \(-5\). The next factor scales the result by \(4\).
In the sum both multipliers are applied to the original vector. The combined values are \(-20\) and \(-1\), respectively.

extraPractice.title: Keep the inverse sign
extraPractice.prompt: Suppose \(A\mathbf v=-6\mathbf v,\quad \mathbf v\ne\mathbf0\) and \(A\) is invertible. Find the eigenvalue of \(A^{-1}\) corresponding to \(\mathbf v\).
extraPractice.hint: Keep the same non-zero eigenvector while changing the matrix.
extraPractice.solution:
Apply \(A^{-1}\) on the left of both sides of the original relation. The scalar still commutes with the matrix.

\(\mathbf v=\lambda A^{-1}\mathbf v\); as \(\lambda\ne0\), divide by \(\lambda\).

Substituting \(\lambda=-6\) gives the associated eigenvalue \(- \frac{1}{6}\).

extraPractice.title: One matrix kills this vector
extraPractice.prompt: The same non-zero vector \(\boldsymbol v\) has eigenvalue \(2\) for \(A\) and \(0\) for \(B\). Find its eigenvalue for \(AB\) and for \(A+B\).
extraPractice.hint: Check that both matrices act on the same vector.
extraPractice.solution:
The rightmost factor \(B\) multiplies the vector by \(0\). The next factor scales the result by \(2\).

In the sum both multipliers are applied to the original vector. The combined values are \(0\) and \(2\), respectively.

extraPractice.title: Reverse the original multiplier
extraPractice.prompt: Let \(A\boldsymbol v=3\boldsymbol v\) for a non-zero vector. Find its eigenvalue for \(-4A+7I\).
extraPractice.hint: Use that the identity leaves each vector unchanged.
extraPractice.solution:
Multiply the original scalar by \(-4\). The identity term adds \(7\) times the original vector.

The combined multiplier is \(-4\times(3)+7=-5\).

extraPractice.title: Check the identity term
extraPractice.prompt: Suppose \(A\mathbf v=-4\mathbf v,\quad \mathbf v\ne\mathbf0\). Find the eigenvalue of \(A^2+A+2I\) corresponding to \(\mathbf v\).
extraPractice.hint: Keep the same non-zero eigenvector while changing the matrix.
extraPractice.solution:
Each matrix term acts on the same vector, so the scalar multipliers can be added.

Use \(A^2\mathbf v=\lambda^2\mathbf v\) and \(I\mathbf v=\mathbf v\).

Substituting \(\lambda=-4\) gives the associated eigenvalue \(14\).

extraPractice.title: Raise to the fourth power
extraPractice.prompt: Suppose \(A\mathbf v=-3\mathbf v,\quad \mathbf v\ne\mathbf0\). Find the eigenvalue of \(A^{4}\) corresponding to \(\mathbf v\).
extraPractice.hint: Keep the same non-zero eigenvector while changing the matrix.
extraPractice.solution:
Apply \(A\) one step at a time. Every application multiplies this same direction by \(\lambda\).

\(A^n\mathbf v=A^{n-1}(\lambda\mathbf v)=\lambda^n\mathbf v\).

Substituting \(\lambda=-3\) gives the associated eigenvalue \(81\).

glossary.definition: A line through the origin whose direction is preserved under the corresponding matrix action.
The operation which undoes an invertible matrix.
A sum of scalar multiples of \(I,A,A^2,\dots\).
A non-zero vector which is an eigenvector for each specified matrix.

revision.body: If \(A\boldsymbol v=\lambda\boldsymbol v\), then \(p(A)\boldsymbol v=p(\lambda)\boldsymbol v\). Invertible \(A\) gives reciprocal eigenvalue \(\frac1\lambda\) for \(A^{-1}\). Only combine actions of two different matrices along a verified shared vector.
revision.checks:
• What is the action of \(A^3\) if \(\lambda=-2\)?
  • Why does \(A^{-1}\) require an invertibility condition?
  • What does \(A+\mu I\) do on the same eigenvector?
revision.examTip: Use the definition on the actual vector. Avoid assuming matrices with a common eigenvector commute.

fp2_matrices2_cayley.description: Use the characteristic polynomial and Cayley–Hamilton identity to reduce matrix powers and derive an inverse.

sections.title: How are the characteristic coefficients organised?
sections.label: Write the monic polynomial
sections.intro: Use a consistent convention before converting characteristic data into a matrix equation. For a two-by-two matrix the trace and determinant give the expansion immediately.

blocks.html: \(p(\lambda)=\lambda^2-\operatorname{tr}(A)\lambda+\det A\) in two dimensions. The three-dimensional polynomial is monic cubic, with constant \(-\det A\).
Coupling a formula written for \(\det(\lambda I-A)\) with the coefficients of \(\det(A-\lambda I)\) gives the wrong signs in odd dimension.
Keep the matrix dimension visible when applying a determinant sign rule.

blocks.title: Match the trace coefficient
blocks.prompt: The characteristic polynomial of \(\left(\begin{matrix}-3 & 0\\16 & 5\end{matrix}\right)\) is \(\lambda^{2} + \lambda c - 15\). Find \(c\).
blocks.hint: Use a monic characteristic polynomial and compare the matching powers.
blocks.solution:
Compute the determinant \(\det(\lambda I-A)\) and expand.

It is \(\lambda^{2} - 2 \lambda - 15\). Match the coefficient of \(\lambda\) to get \(-2\).

blocks.title: Recover a cubic coefficient
blocks.prompt: The characteristic polynomial of \(\left(\begin{matrix}-3 & 0 & 8\\-5 & 2 & 5\\0 & 0 & 5\end{matrix}\right)\) is \(\lambda^{3} + \lambda^{2} c - 11 \lambda + 30\). Find \(c\).
blocks.hint: Use a monic characteristic polynomial and compare the matching powers.
blocks.solution:
Compute the determinant \(\det(\lambda I-A)\) and expand.

It is \(\lambda^{3} - 4 \lambda^{2} - 11 \lambda + 30\). Match the coefficient of \(\lambda^{2}\) to get \(-4\).

sections.title: Why does the polynomial vanish at the matrix?
sections.label: Cayley–Hamilton
sections.intro: For the distinct real eigenvalues here, an eigenbasis spans the entire space. The polynomial action sends each basis vector to zero, which is enough to determine the whole matrix.

blocks.html: If \(p\) is the characteristic polynomial then \(p(A)=0\). A constant term of \(p\) becomes a multiple of \(I\) and the right-hand side is the zero matrix.
Replacing a constant by a matrix whose entries are all that number changes its action. Only multiply the identity.
Write the matrix identity with \(I\) and \(0\) clearly identified.

blocks.title: Use the characteristic recurrence
blocks.prompt: For \(A=\left(\begin{matrix}-2 & 0 & 5\\-3 & 1 & 3\\0 & 0 & 3\end{matrix}\right)\), determine the entry in row 3, column 1 of \(A^{6}\).
blocks.hint: Reduce the power using the characteristic equation before multiplying matrices.
blocks.solution:
The characteristic polynomial is \(\lambda^{3} - 2 \lambda^{2} - 5 \lambda + 6\). By Cayley–Hamilton its value at the matrix is the zero matrix.

Dividing the scalar polynomial \(\lambda^{6}\) by the characteristic polynomial leaves remainder \(77 \lambda^{2} + 56 \lambda - 132\). Thus \(A^{6}=77 A^{2} + 56 A - 132 I\), using the identity matrix for the constant term.

Evaluating this identity gives \(\left(\begin{matrix}64 & 0 & 665\\63 & 1 & -63\\0 & 0 & 729\end{matrix}\right)\). Read the requested entry by row, then column.

sections.title: How do I reduce higher powers with the characteristic equation?
sections.label: Reduce a high power
sections.intro: An identity between powers lets you replace a high power by a combination of lower powers. Polynomial division avoids repeated large matrix products.

blocks.html: Divide the scalar polynomial \(\lambda^k\) by \(p(\lambda)\). If the remainder is \(r\), then \(A^k=r(A)\). All higher-order terms in the quotient multiply \(p(A)=0\).
The polynomial rule only makes the quotient contribution zero after substitution of the matrix. A numeric eigenvalue is not needed to compute the remainder.
Write the scalar division or use the characteristic recurrence; then evaluate the lower powers.

blocks.title: Reduce the power of a 2D matrix
blocks.prompt: For \(A=\left(\begin{matrix}9 & -5\\10 & -6\end{matrix}\right)\), determine the entry in row 2, column 1 of \(A^{3}\).
blocks.hint: Reduce the power using the characteristic equation before multiplying matrices.
blocks.solution:
The characteristic polynomial is \(\lambda^{2} - 3 \lambda - 4\). By Cayley–Hamilton its value at the matrix is the zero matrix.

Dividing the scalar polynomial \(\lambda^{3}\) by the characteristic polynomial leaves remainder \(13 \lambda + 12\). Thus \(A^{3}=13 A + 12 I\), using the identity matrix for the constant term.

Evaluating this identity gives \(\left(\begin{matrix}129 & -65\\130 & -66\end{matrix}\right)\). Read the requested entry by row, then column.

blocks.title: Reduce the power of a 3D matrix
blocks.prompt: For \(A=\left(\begin{matrix}-1 & 0 & 0\\-6 & 2 & 0\\12 & -3 & 5\end{matrix}\right)\), determine the entry in row 2, column 3 of \(A^{5}\).
blocks.hint: Reduce the power using the characteristic equation before multiplying matrices.
blocks.solution:
The characteristic polynomial is \(\lambda^{3} - 6 \lambda^{2} + 3 \lambda + 10\). By Cayley–Hamilton its value at the matrix is the zero matrix.

Dividing the scalar polynomial \(\lambda^{5}\) by the characteristic polynomial leaves remainder \(170 \lambda^{2} - 159 \lambda - 330\). Thus \(A^{5}=170 A^{2} - 159 A - 330 I\), using the identity matrix for the constant term.

Evaluating this identity gives \(\left(\begin{matrix}-1 & 0 & 0\\-66 & 32 & 0\\9312 & -3093 & 3125\end{matrix}\right)\). Read the requested entry by row, then column.

sections.title: When does the identity also give the inverse?
sections.label: Recover the inverse
sections.intro: A non-zero constant term means the characteristic polynomial does not have zero as a root. Then the matrix identity can be rearranged to find a formula for the inverse.

blocks.html: If \(A^2-sA+dI=0\) with \(d\ne0\), multiplication by \(A^{-1}\) gives \(A-sI+dA^{-1}=0\). Thus \(A^{-1}=\frac{sI-A}{d}\).
Multiplying by an inverse is invalid if the characteristic constant is zero.
Check your expression by multiplying by the original matrix.

blocks.title: Use a nonzero determinant
blocks.prompt: For \(A=\left(\begin{matrix}-14 & 18\\-9 & 13\end{matrix}\right)\), use the characteristic equation to find the entry in row 2, column 1 of \(A^{-1}\).
blocks.hint: Multiply the matrix identity by the inverse only after justifying that it exists.
blocks.solution:
The characteristic equation is \(\lambda^{2} + \lambda - 20=0\). Its constant term is \(-20\), so zero is not an eigenvalue.

Replace the scalar variable with \(A\) and the constant term with its multiple of \(I\). Multiply the matrix identity by \(A^{-1}\).

Solving for the inverse gives \(\left(\begin{matrix}- \frac{13}{20} & \frac{9}{10}\\- \frac{9}{20} & \frac{7}{10}\end{matrix}\right)\). The requested entry is \(- \frac{9}{20}\).

sections.title: Which approach is shortest for a requested matrix entry?
sections.label: Choose a calculation
sections.intro: If only one entry is required, reduce the power first. Evaluate only the matching entries of the remaining powers.

blocks.html: In two dimensions the remainder has form \(u\lambda+v\). The target entry is \(u A_{ij}+v I_{ij}\). A constant affects a diagonal entry only.
For an off-diagonal entry \(I_{ij}=0\), even if \(v\) is nonzero.
Give enough working to justify the reduced power before reading off the requested entry.

blocks.title: Evaluate only the requested entry
blocks.prompt: For \(A=\left(\begin{matrix}-2 & 0\\10 & 3\end{matrix}\right)\), determine the entry in row 2, column 1 of \(A^{4}\).
blocks.hint: Reduce the power using the characteristic equation before multiplying matrices.
blocks.solution:
The characteristic polynomial is \(\lambda^{2} - \lambda - 6\). By Cayley–Hamilton its value at the matrix is the zero matrix.

Dividing the scalar polynomial \(\lambda^{4}\) by the characteristic polynomial leaves remainder \(13 \lambda + 42\). Thus \(A^{4}=13 A + 42 I\), using the identity matrix for the constant term.

Evaluating this identity gives \(\left(\begin{matrix}16 & 0\\130 & 81\end{matrix}\right)\). Read the requested entry by row, then column.

examples.title: Write the cubic matrix identity

examples.title: Use a quadratic remainder

examples.title: Reduce with a cubic characteristic polynomial
examples.question: For \(A=\left(\begin{matrix}-1 & 0 & 4\\-3 & 2 & 3\\0 & 0 & 3\end{matrix}\right)\), determine the entry in row 3, column 1 of \(A^{6}\).
solution: The characteristic polynomial is \(\lambda^{3} - 4 \lambda^{2} + \lambda + 6\). By Cayley–Hamilton its value at the matrix is the zero matrix.

Dividing the scalar polynomial \(\lambda^{6}\) by the characteristic polynomial leaves remainder \(161 \lambda^{2} - 140 \lambda - 300\). Thus \(A^{6}=161 A^{2} - 140 A - 300 I\), using the identity matrix for the constant term.

examples.title: Find an inverse entry without cofactors
examples.question: For \(A=\left(\begin{matrix}7 & -5\\10 & -8\end{matrix}\right)\), use the characteristic equation to find the entry in row 1, column 2 of \(A^{-1}\).
solution: The characteristic equation is \(\lambda^{2} + \lambda - 6=0\). Its constant term is \(-6\), so zero is not an eigenvalue.
Replace the scalar variable with \(A\) and the constant term with its multiple of \(I\). Multiply the matrix identity by \(A^{-1}\).

examples.title: Read one off-diagonal entry of a high power
examples.question: For \(A=\left(\begin{matrix}-3 & 0\\10 & 2\end{matrix}\right)\), determine the entry in row 2, column 1 of \(A^{4}\).

Evaluating this identity gives \(\left(\begin{matrix}81 & 0\\-130 & 16\end{matrix}\right)\). Read the requested entry by row, then column.

glossary.definition: The polynomial \(p(\lambda)=\det(\lambda I-A)\).
\(p(A)=0\) for the characteristic polynomial of \(A\).

revision.body: The constant term is multiplied by \(I\). If \(p(A)=0\), use the scalar remainder of \(\lambda^k\) modulo \(p\) to reduce \(A^k\). For a \(2\times2\) matrix with nonzero determinant, \(A^{-1}=\frac{\operatorname{tr}(A)I-A}{\det A}\).

fp2_matrices2_diagonal.description: Diagonalise a matrix and use matched eigenvector columns to compute powers, vector images and square roots.

sections.title: How do Q and D record a change of basis?
sections.label: Match columns to values
sections.intro: Read \(AQ\) by columns. Its first column is the image of the first column of \(Q\). Each such image must be the same column multiplied by its eigenvalue.

blocks.html: If \(Q=(\boldsymbol v_1\ \boldsymbol v_2\ \cdots)\) and \(D\) has the matching eigenvalues down its diagonal, then \(AQ=QD\). Independent eigenvectors make \(Q\) invertible, hence \(A=QDQ^{-1}\).
The matching order matters. Swapping two columns of \(Q\) without swapping the corresponding entries of \(D\) describes a different matrix.
Check the identity \(AQ=QD\) before doing a large power.

blocks.title: A signed integer power
blocks.prompt: For \(Q=\left(\begin{matrix}1 & 0\\-2 & 1\end{matrix}\right)\) with matching \(D=\left(\begin{matrix}-2 & 0\\0 & 5\end{matrix}\right)\), let \(A=QDQ^{-1}\). Find entry \((2,1)\) of \(A^{3}\).
blocks.hint: Raise the diagonal entries to the power, maintaining the order of eigenvectors.
blocks.solution:
Each copy of \(Q^{-1}Q\) cancels to the identity inside the product. Hence \(A^{3}=QD^{3}Q^{-1}\).

The diagonal matrix becomes \(\left(\begin{matrix}-8 & 0\\0 & 125\end{matrix}\right)\). Multiplying left by \(Q\) and right by \(Q^{-1}\) gives \(\left(\begin{matrix}-8 & 0\\266 & 125\end{matrix}\right)\).

blocks.title: Match the other basis order
blocks.prompt: For \(Q=\left(\begin{matrix}2 & 1\\1 & 1\end{matrix}\right)\) with matching \(D=\left(\begin{matrix}-3 & 0\\0 & 4\end{matrix}\right)\), let \(A=QDQ^{-1}\). Find entry \((1,2)\) of \(A^{4}\).
blocks.hint: Raise the diagonal entries to the power, maintaining the order of eigenvectors.
blocks.solution:
Each copy of \(Q^{-1}Q\) cancels to the identity inside the product. Hence \(A^{4}=QD^{4}Q^{-1}\).

The diagonal matrix becomes \(\left(\begin{matrix}81 & 0\\0 & 256\end{matrix}\right)\). Multiplying left by \(Q\) and right by \(Q^{-1}\) gives \(\left(\begin{matrix}-94 & 350\\-175 & 431\end{matrix}\right)\).

sections.title: Why can I take powers of the diagonal entries only?
sections.label: Cancel interior factors
sections.intro: Write out two copies of \(QDQ^{-1}\) side by side. The nearby inverse and basis factors cancel in the middle.

blocks.html: \(A^k=QD^kQ^{-1}\) for nonnegative integers \(k\). If all eigenvalues are nonzero, the formula also holds for negative integers.
Taking powers of \(Q\) and \(Q^{-1}\) separately fails because the matrices do not usually commute.
At \(k=0\) the expression reduces to \(QI Q^{-1}=I\).

blocks.title: Reduce the third power
blocks.prompt: For \(Q=\left(\begin{matrix}0 & 1\\1 & -2\end{matrix}\right)\) with matching \(D=\left(\begin{matrix}-1 & 0\\0 & 4\end{matrix}\right)\), let \(A=QDQ^{-1}\). Find entry \((2,1)\) of \(A^{3}\).
blocks.hint: Raise the diagonal entries to the power, maintaining the order of eigenvectors.
blocks.solution:
Each copy of \(Q^{-1}Q\) cancels to the identity inside the product. Hence \(A^{3}=QD^{3}Q^{-1}\).

The diagonal matrix becomes \(\left(\begin{matrix}-1 & 0\\0 & 64\end{matrix}\right)\). Multiplying left by \(Q\) and right by \(Q^{-1}\) gives \(\left(\begin{matrix}64 & 0\\-130 & -1\end{matrix}\right)\).

sections.title: How do I calculate a selected entry efficiently?
sections.label: Read the needed product
sections.intro: After taking the individual powers, each column of \(Q\) is multiplied by its matching diagonal entry. The final multiplication combines these columns.

blocks.html: For entry \(i,j\), use row \(i\) of \(QD^k\) and column \(j\) of \(Q^{-1}\). This avoids calculating unrequested entries.
The entry at row \(i\), column \(j\) uses row from the left factor and column from the right factor.
Very different sizes or signs in the powers can cancel. Keep exact arithmetic until the end.

blocks.title: Only one entry is required
blocks.prompt: For \(Q=\left(\begin{matrix}1 & -1\\2 & -1\end{matrix}\right)\) with matching \(D=\left(\begin{matrix}-1 & 0\\0 & 5\end{matrix}\right)\), let \(A=QDQ^{-1}\). Find entry \((2,1)\) of \(A^{5}\).
blocks.hint: Raise the diagonal entries to the power, maintaining the order of eigenvectors.

Each copy of \(Q^{-1}Q\) cancels to the identity inside the product. Hence \(A^{5}=QD^{5}Q^{-1}\).

The diagonal matrix becomes \(\left(\begin{matrix}-1 & 0\\0 & 3125\end{matrix}\right)\). Multiplying left by \(Q\) and right by \(Q^{-1}\) gives \(\left(\begin{matrix}6251 & -3126\\6252 & -3127\end{matrix}\right)\).

blocks.title: An entry in three dimensions
blocks.prompt: For \(Q=\left(\begin{matrix}1 & 0 & 0\\2 & 1 & 0\\-1 & 1 & 1\end{matrix}\right)\) with matching \(D=\left(\begin{matrix}-2 & 0 & 0\\0 & 1 & 0\\0 & 0 & 5\end{matrix}\right)\), let \(A=QDQ^{-1}\). Find entry \((2,3)\) of \(A^{3}\).
blocks.hint: Raise the diagonal entries to the power, maintaining the order of eigenvectors.

sections.title: What if I only need the image of one vector?
sections.label: Apply a power to a vector
sections.intro: Read the factors from right to left. Find the input coordinates in the eigenbasis, scale those coordinates, and then convert back.

blocks.html: \(\boldsymbol w=Q^{-1}\boldsymbol u\) gives eigenbasis coordinates. Then \(A^k\boldsymbol u=Q(D^k\boldsymbol w)\).
The vector \(D^k Q^{-1}\boldsymbol u\) is still measured in the eigenbasis. A final multiplication by \(Q\) is needed.
If the input already lies on one eigenvector, use its single scalar multiplier directly.

blocks.title: Return to the original coordinates
blocks.prompt: Let \(Q=\left(\begin{matrix}2 & 1\\1 & 1\end{matrix}\right)\) with matching \(D=\left(\begin{matrix}-2 & 0\\0 & 3\end{matrix}\right)\). If \(A=QDQ^{-1}\), find \(A^{4}\mathbf u\) for \(\mathbf u=\left(\begin{matrix}3\\4\end{matrix}\right)\).
blocks.hint: Apply the factors from right to left to a vector.
blocks.solution:
First express the input vector in the eigenbasis. This gives \(Q^{-1}\mathbf u=\left(\begin{matrix}-1\\5\end{matrix}\right)\).

Multiply the coordinates by \(D^{4}\) and return to the original basis using \(Q\). The resulting vector is \(\left(\begin{matrix}373\\389\end{matrix}\right)\).

sections.title: How can a diagonal form guide a matrix square root?
sections.label: Choose eigenvalue signs
sections.intro: A diagonal square root can be constructed by selecting a square root for each diagonal entry. Conjugating back gives a corresponding matrix square root.

blocks.html: If \(A=QDQ^{-1}\) and \(E^2=D\), then \((QEQ^{-1})^2=A\). The question may specify signs or impose other restrictions to select a particular root.
Squaring loses eigenvalue signs. Positive diagonal entries of \(D\) do not require positive eigenvalues of every root.
Verify a proposed root by squaring it using the same basis.

blocks.title: Read the chosen root sign
blocks.prompt: A matrix \(B\) satisfies \(B^2=\left(\begin{matrix}-7 & 16\\-32 & 41\end{matrix}\right)\). It has \(Q=\left(\begin{matrix}1 & 1\\1 & 2\end{matrix}\right)\) as its eigenvector basis. It has the following eigenvalues in the same order as these columns: \(-3\), \(5\). Find entry \((1,2)\) of \(B\).

fields.label: Requested entry of the square root

blocks.hint: Select the diagonal signs according to the eigenvalue information.
blocks.solution:
The given eigenvalues already choose the square-root signs. Use \(D=\left(\begin{matrix}-3 & 0\\0 & 5\end{matrix}\right)\) with the stated eigenbasis.

Then \(B=QDQ^{-1}=\left(\begin{matrix}-11 & 8\\-16 & 13\end{matrix}\right)\). Squaring this expression recovers the original matrix.

examples.title: Compute one off-diagonal entry
examples.question: For \(Q=\left(\begin{matrix}0 & 1\\1 & -2\end{matrix}\right)\) with matching \(D=\left(\begin{matrix}2 & 0\\0 & -3\end{matrix}\right)\), let \(A=QDQ^{-1}\). Find entry \((2,1)\) of \(A^{3}\).
